changes.before: You know GF9. Here is what changes.
changes.after: About this guide

changes.before: The starting point
changes.after: For players who know GF9

changes.before: This book assumes you already play Gale Force Nine's 2019 Dune. It compares that game with the 2026 second edition. Use it to replace old habits, check your faction, and identify the changed components. Keep the full 2.0 rulebook beside it for ordinary rules.
changes.after: This guide compares Gale Force Nine's 2019 Dune with the 2026 second edition. It covers changed rules, faction abilities and components. Use the full 2.0 rulebook for rules that have stayed the same.

changes.before: Basic and Advanced are different baselines
changes.after: Basic and Advanced

changes.before: The new default combines elements that used to be split between Basic and Advanced. A Basic player gains city income, advanced faction powers and a spice decision in battle. An Advanced player replaces the old support arithmetic and two-pile Spice procedure. Simply saying "play Advanced" misses those changes.
changes.after: The new default game combines parts of the old Basic and Advanced rules. Basic players gain city income, Advanced faction abilities and spice spending in battle. Advanced players replace spice support and the two-pile Spice deck procedure.

changes.before: How to use this guide
changes.after: Unresolved rules

changes.before: Confirmed rules are the main lesson. Boxes labeled "Open wording" retain genuine source conflicts. The expansion appendix distinguishes announced revisions from complete rules. Those boxes are review questions, not invented house rules.
changes.after: Boxes marked "Open wording" describe passages that conflict or leave a rule unclear. The expansion appendix covers announced changes for which complete rules are still missing.

changes.before: What counts as a difference
changes.after: Which earlier rules?

changes.before: The old printed book, its later official FAQ and Dune Zone's existing GF9 books are separate comparisons. When a clarification was already in our old book, it is labeled "Already familiar". When 2.0 reverses our adopted reading, that is stated explicitly.
changes.after: The 2019 rulebook, its later FAQ and Dune Zone's GF9 books sometimes differ. A rule marked "Already familiar" was already in Dune Zone's earlier books. Changes to a Dune Zone ruling are identified separately from changes to the original printing.

before: The earlier Basic game, with later clarifications identified.
The earlier Advanced rules, including half-strength unsupported forces.
The optional restoration of old spice-support combat.
A designer describes a revision, but complete replacement rules are still missing.
after: The 2019 Basic rules, with later clarifications identified.
The 2019 Advanced rules, including half-strength unsupported forces.

changes.before: Sources for review
changes.after: Page and edition references

changes.before: Page references mean printed source PDF pages counted from the cover. Publication Edition numbers on dune.zone identify website versions, not the game edition. This guide uses our older publication Edition 2 books and the 2.0 publication Edition 3, pinned in the research dossier.
changes.after: Page references count from the cover of each source PDF. Edition numbers on dune.zone are website versions. This comparison uses Edition 2 of the earlier books and Edition 3 of the 2.0 book, as recorded in the accompanying research files.

changes.before: GF9 dealt traitors before the starting Treachery cards. In 2.0, deal the starting Treachery cards first, then choose a traitor. This gives you your initial hand information during that choice. Harkonnen still starts with two Treachery cards; that count is not new.
changes.after: Starting Treachery cards are now dealt before players choose their traitors. Previously, traitors came first. You can now consider your starting hand when choosing a traitor. Harkonnen still starts with two Treachery cards.

changes.before: Safe traitors were already allowed
changes.after: Choosing your own leader as a traitor

changes.before: You may choose one of your own leaders as your safe traitor. This differs from the condition in the original 2019 setup paragraph, but the later FAQ and our GF9 book already allowed it. Harkonnen now has a separate own-traitor redraw, covered on its faction page.
changes.after: You may choose one of your own leaders as a safe traitor. The original 2019 setup paragraph restricted this choice, but the later FAQ and Dune Zone's GF9 book already allowed it. Harkonnen's new redraw is covered on its faction page.

changes.before: The new prediction-card selection method says start with the lowest card, but calls the order descending. Those instructions disagree. Random faction assignment remains available; this guide does not silently repair the sentence.
changes.after: The prediction-card method says to start with the lowest card, then describes the order as descending. The two instructions conflict. Random faction assignment is still available.

changes.before: Same place, new name
changes.after: Renamed places and cards

changes.before: Cave of Birds is the renamed southwest stronghold. It is not an extra stronghold. Kinetic still matches the relevant weapon and defense categories. Harj is the printed name of the familiar extra-movement card; it is not a second card.
changes.after: Cave of Birds is the former Habbanya Sietch stronghold in the southwest. Kinetic replaces projectile as a weapon and defense type. Harj is the printed name of the old Hajr card and has the same extra-movement effect.

changes.before: Starting resources do change
changes.after: Starting resources

changes.before: Fremen starts with four spice instead of three. Guild starts with eight spice and all twenty forces in reserves, then makes a compulsory paid setup shipment instead of receiving five forces fixed in Tuek's. Leader changes have their own reference page.
changes.after: Fremen starts with four spice instead of three. Guild starts with eight spice and all twenty forces in reserves, then pays for a setup shipment. Previously it received five forces in Tuek's Sietch. Leader changes are listed on the roster page.

changes.before: Use the Storm deck every game
changes.after: The Storm deck

changes.before: Ordinary later storms used two players' dials. The six-card Storm deck was tied to Advanced Fremen. Its cards were returned and shuffled through that faction's procedure.
changes.after: After the first storm placement, two players normally dialed the storm's movement. The six-card Storm deck was an Advanced Fremen ability, with its own procedure for returning and shuffling cards.

changes.before: After the first storm placement, use the shared nine-card Storm deck whether or not Fremen is playing. Draw into a discard pile. Three cards instruct you to reshuffle the discarded cards after moving the storm. Read the drawn instruction instead of automatically dialing every round.
changes.after: After the first storm placement, use the shared nine-card Storm deck, even without Fremen. Draw each card into a discard pile and follow its instruction. Three cards require the discards to be reshuffled after the storm moves.

changes.before: One card calls for the two players who last used Battle Wheels to dial 1-3 each. If there was no battle in the previous round, use the specified factions beside the storm. The initial placement still uses the separate 0-20 dials.
changes.after: The dial card tells the two players who last used Battle Wheels to dial 1-3 each. If no battle took place in the previous round, use the factions beside the storm as specified on the card. The initial storm placement still uses 0-20 dials.

changes.before: Different deal rules
changes.after: Deals during storm movement

changes.before: The first storm placement explicitly forbids coordination. The later dial card explicitly allows deals and bribes. Do not treat those two occasions as the same procedure.
changes.after: Players cannot coordinate their dials for the first storm placement. Deals and bribes are allowed when the later dial card is drawn.

changes.before: Fremen no longer selects and recycles a private card to set the next movement. At the end of Storm, it inspects the top Storm card under Storm Insight. This is advance knowledge of the shared deck.
changes.after: At the end of Storm, Fremen uses Storm Insight to inspect the top card of the shared deck. It no longer selects and recycles a private card to set the next movement.

changes.before: Rivals protected under the same storm
changes.after: Battles in a protected sector

changes.before: Two rivals in the same stormed sector of a rock or stronghold now battle. The old FAQ prohibited battles under storm even there. If only one side is in storm, or storm separates the groups, the restriction still applies.
changes.after: Rivals in the same storm-covered sector of rock or a stronghold now battle. The old FAQ prohibited this. Battles are still prevented if only one side is in storm or the storm separates the groups.

changes.before: A small first-player clarification
changes.after: A marker under the storm

changes.before: If the storm is exactly on your faction marker, you are last in storm order. This makes the old "next approached" rule explicit.
changes.after: A faction whose marker is exactly under the storm acts last in storm order. This clarifies the old instruction to start with the marker the storm next approaches.

changes.before: No probability claim
changes.after: Storm deck contents

changes.before: The source gives nine cards, three reshuffle instructions and a dial card. This guide does not invent the complete face distribution or card-counting probabilities.
changes.after: The rulebook identifies nine cards, three reshuffle instructions and a dial card. It does not list all nine card faces.

changes.before: Basic drew a single-territory card. Advanced resolved two separate draws and two discard piles, with independent worm histories.
changes.after: Basic used single-territory cards. Advanced drew twice, using two discard piles and a separate worm history for each pile.

changes.before: A normal Spice card names two territories. Place both blows from that one card, checking each affected sector for storm. Keep one discard pile. Do not draw two new double-Blow cards as though you were still using the old Advanced procedure.
changes.after: Each normal Spice card names two territories. Place both blows, checking each affected sector for storm, and use one discard pile. One paired card replaces the two draws of the old Advanced procedure.

changes.before: A single published card now supplies Hagga Basin and Cielago Depression.
changes.after: Hagga Basin and Cielago Depression share one Spice card.

changes.before: The next ordinary worm
changes.after: A worm after a paired blow

changes.before: Suppose the previous normal card placed spice in Hagga Basin and Cielago Depression. Shai-Hulud threatens the remaining spice and forces in both of those territories, subject to faction protection. Continue replacement draws until an ordinary Spice Blows card appears.
changes.after: If the previous normal card placed spice in Hagga Basin and Cielago Depression, Shai-Hulud threatens the remaining spice and forces in both territories. Faction protection still applies. Draw replacements until an ordinary Spice Blows card appears.

changes.before: One top-card inspection now reveals the next pair, or the coming special event. Under old Advanced play the top card did not reveal both independent upcoming blows.
changes.after: Inspecting the top card now reveals both upcoming blows, or a special event. In old Advanced play, it revealed only one of the two independent draws.

changes.before: More than one location can be involved in the same worm event. Use the revised Call Sandworms and ally-riding rules, rather than resetting the old two-pile procedure.
changes.after: One worm event can affect more than one location. Fremen uses the revised Call Sandworms and ally-riding rules with the single discard pile.

changes.before: The source includes Little Maker among prior blows a later worm can affect, but does not fully explain recording the chosen location and intervening special discards. Keep the chosen marker visible in examples; do not assume the worm skips back to the previous normal pair.
changes.after: The rulebook includes Little Maker among earlier blows that a later worm can affect. It leaves parts of the discard sequence and location tracking unexplained. Keep the chosen location marked; the text does not say to skip it and use the previous normal pair.

changes.before: Little Maker is a different event
changes.after: Little Maker

changes.before: 2019 pp5,8,13; second edition pp7,11. Card artwork is the existing production asset.
changes.after: 2019 pp5,8,13; second edition pp7,11.

changes.before: The last player in storm order chooses an eligible empty Spice Blow marker outside storm and places ten spice there. Then a Nexus occurs. No forces or spice are devoured and nobody rides this event as a worm.
changes.after: The last player in storm order places ten spice on an eligible empty Spice Blow marker outside storm. A Nexus follows. Little Maker devours no forces or spice and cannot be ridden.

changes.before: Recognize the card
changes.after: A new Spice card

changes.before: Little Maker is neither Shai-Hulud nor the older expansion cards Sandtrout and Great Maker. Those names have different effects. The base Spice deck now has sixteen cards rather than twenty-one.
changes.after: Little Maker is a separate card from Shai-Hulud and the older expansion cards Sandtrout and Great Maker. Each has a different effect. The base Spice deck now contains sixteen cards instead of twenty-one.

changes.before: Shai-Hulud is still the worm event. Little Maker does not trigger abilities that require Shai-Hulud.
changes.after: Shai-Hulud triggers worm abilities. Little Maker does not.

changes.before: Round one sets aside non-normal-Blow cards and reshuffles them afterward. It does not produce a first-round Little Maker Nexus.
changes.after: Set it aside with the other non-normal-Blow cards and reshuffle them afterward. Little Maker does not cause a Nexus in round one.

changes.before: Discard it without effect and continue the worm's replacement draws. Do not add its ten spice or another Nexus in that sequence.
changes.after: Discard it without effect and continue drawing replacements. It adds neither ten spice nor another Nexus during this sequence.

changes.before: A useful distinction
changes.after: Alliances without a worm

changes.before: The new card can give an extra chance to change alliances without creating worm destruction or a ride. That is the rule difference; it is not a promise that a particular game will have more successful Fremen rides.
changes.after: Little Maker gives players an opportunity to form or break alliances without losing forces or spice to a worm. Fremen cannot use this event for a worm ride.

changes.before: Remember the pair
changes.after: Paired locations

changes.before: The normal deck now has nine paired cards showing eighteen locations. Other listed old blow amounts are retained. A later ordinary worm can threaten both sites of a pair, so the pairing is useful information, not just a condensed deck.
changes.after: The nine normal Spice cards show eighteen locations. Apart from the changes in the table, the old blow amounts stay the same. The pairing also determines which two territories a later Shai-Hulud can affect.

changes.before: Component reference
changes.after: Normal Spice Blows

changes.before: This table comes from the supplied second-edition card sheet and the old printed board. It gives normal blow locations, not a rule that spice can never appear elsewhere through an effect.
changes.after: These locations and amounts come from the second-edition card sheet and the old board. Card and faction effects may place spice elsewhere.

changes.before: Find the revised Spice sites
changes.after: New Spice Blow locations

changes.before: The three newly used normal blow territories are highlighted. This familiar map retains the earlier labels; Cave of Birds is the name mapping explained beside it.
changes.after: The Greater Flat, Cielago Depression and Cielago East are highlighted. This map uses the old name Habbanya Sietch for Cave of Birds.

changes.before: The Greater Flat now has a seven-spice normal blow; Cielago Depression and Cielago East each have eight. They pair with Red Chasm, Hagga Basin and Wind Pass North respectively.
changes.after: The Greater Flat has a seven-spice blow. Cielago Depression and Cielago East each have eight. Their paired locations are Red Chasm, Hagga Basin and Wind Pass North respectively.

changes.before: A name mapping, not a new stronghold
changes.after: Cave of Birds

changes.before: The existing production map calls the southwest stronghold Habbanya Sietch. The second-edition source calls that same place Cave of Birds. Read that name mapping wherever it affects a faction condition.
changes.after: Cave of Birds is called Habbanya Sietch on this map. Both names refer to the same southwest stronghold, including when checking faction victory conditions.

changes.before: Read the card for the amount
changes.after: Changed amounts

changes.before: Four old blow amounts also decrease. The preceding table lists them. Reusing the familiar map picture does not restore the old printed spice values.
changes.after: Broken Land, The Great Flat, South Mesa and Habbanya Ridge Flat have smaller blows. Use the new card amounts listed on the preceding page, even when playing on an older board.

changes.before: Spice adds strength to your force dial
changes.after: Spice strength in battle

changes.before: An ordinary committed force contributed one strength, with no battle-spice decision.
changes.after: An ordinary force contributed one strength without spending spice.

changes.before: A force needed one spice to count at full strength. Unsupported forces counted at half strength, including the appropriate special-force values. Committing more forces without enough spice did not give the same strength as supporting them all.
changes.after: Each force needed one spice to fight at full strength. Unsupported forces fought at half strength, with the appropriate values for special forces.

changes.before: Start with full dialed force strength. You may buy one spice-strength tier if your force dial reaches its threshold. Add that bonus and a surviving leader's strength. The bonus does not consume extra force tokens.
changes.after: Forces fight at full strength. You may spend spice for one strength bonus, provided your dial meets that bonus's threshold. Add the bonus and any surviving leader's strength to your force strength. The spice bonus costs no additional forces.

changes.before: The old Advanced support system survives as Classic Spice Dialing. Select that variant explicitly. The default rules on this page do not use half-strength unsupported forces.
changes.after: Classic Spice Dialing uses the old Advanced support system. Choose this variant before play. Under the default 2.0 rules, unsupported forces no longer fight at half strength.

changes.before: With no spice, four committed ordinary forces contribute 4 in 2.0. With four spice, they contribute 6. Under old Advanced rules, those four supported forces contributed 4. With no support at all, the same four tokens contributed 2.
changes.after: Four ordinary forces contribute 4 strength without spice, or 6 after spending four spice. Under old Advanced rules, the same four forces contributed 4 with full support or 2 without support.

changes.before: Choose a tier, not several purchases
changes.after: Buy one bonus

changes.before: Dialing eight permits +1, +2 or +3 at the respective costs. You cannot buy +3 and +1 together. The cost progression is 2, 4, 8; it is not one spice per extra strength.
changes.after: A force dial of eight allows a +1, +2 or +3 bonus at a cost of 2, 4 or 8 spice. Choose one bonus; they cannot be combined.

changes.before: Count strength, not tokens
changes.after: Thresholds use force strength

changes.before: One Sardaukar is normally two force strength, enough to qualify for +1 at a cost of two spice. Its special exception against Fremen still applies.
changes.after: One Sardaukar normally contributes two force strength. That qualifies for a +1 bonus at a cost of two spice. Its special exception against Fremen still applies.

changes.before: Same commitment, different total
changes.after: Battle strength example

changes.before: Compare the same four ordinary forces
changes.after: Four ordinary forces and four spice

changes.before: The following wheels use the same force dial and four spice. The old Advanced calculation supports all four forces for 4 strength. The new calculation adds a +2 bonus, for 6 before leaders.
changes.after: The left wheel uses the old Advanced rules: four spice supports four ordinary forces for 4 strength. The right wheel uses 2.0: four spice buys a +2 bonus, giving the same forces 6 strength before adding a leader.

changes.before: Add the same surviving leader
changes.after: Add a strength-3 leader

changes.before: With a strength-3 leader on each plan, the old Advanced total is 7 and the 2.0 total is 9. Those are two versions of the same side's plan, not opponents in an actual battle.
changes.after: If the leader survives, the old Advanced plan totals 7 and the 2.0 plan totals 9. The wheels show the same player under each edition, rather than two opposing Battle Plans.

changes.before: Losses follow the force contribution
changes.after: Force losses

changes.before: If this 2.0 plan wins, it loses four ordinary forces, not six. The two points bought with spice do not become extra casualties. Losing still removes the faction's forces in the territory under the normal result rules.
changes.after: If the 2.0 plan wins, the player loses four ordinary forces. The +2 spice bonus adds no losses. A losing player still loses their forces in the territory under the normal battle rules.

changes.before: The force dial matters twice
changes.after: The dial sets the maximum bonus

changes.before: It is both committed force strength and access to a spice tier. Having eight forces available does not unlock +3 if you dial only four. A doubled special force contributes its force strength toward the threshold.
changes.after: Having eight forces in the territory does not qualify you for +3 if you dial only four. Special forces count at their force strength when checking the threshold.

changes.before: Reading the diagrams
changes.after: What the wheels show

changes.before: The diagrams compare one side under two editions. They are not opposing plans. The surviving leader is excluded from the pictures and added in the calculation above.
changes.after: Both wheels show a force dial of 4. The leader is left out of the pictures and added in the example above.

changes.before: Commit spice, reveal, then settle
changes.after: Paying for battle spice

changes.before: The new payment
changes.after: Payment at reveal

changes.before: Keep the selected spice tier secret on the wheel until simultaneous reveal, then pay its cost to the Spice Bank. You must have spendable spice already. A general ally contribution and a leader bounty earned from this battle cannot fund it.
changes.after: Choose your spice bonus secretly on the wheel, then pay the Spice Bank when plans are revealed. You must already have the spice available. An ordinary allied contribution or a bounty from this battle cannot pay for it.

changes.before: Specific exceptions matter
changes.after: Faction and card exceptions

changes.before: Fremen receives its qualifying spice strength for free. Emperor halves its ally's cost. Solaris pays the cost from the Bank. These are separate exceptions to the shared payment rule; they are not permission for every ally to fund battle spice.
changes.after: Fremen receives its qualifying bonus for free. Emperor halves its ally's cost. Solaris pays from the Spice Bank. These exceptions do not allow other allies to pay for battle spice.

changes.before: A tempting wrong payment
changes.after: A bounty cannot fund the plan

changes.before: You expect to kill a strength-5 leader, but have no spendable spice. That future bounty cannot buy the +2 tier while you form your plan. Deferred bribes in front of your screen cannot buy it either.
changes.after: You have no spendable spice and expect to kill a strength-5 leader. That bounty cannot pay for a +2 bonus in this battle. Bribes waiting in front of your screen are also unavailable.

changes.before: Traitor results keep their asymmetry
changes.after: Traitor calls

changes.before: The traitor winner keeps its committed spice and loses nothing under that result. The betrayed side loses its committed spice. With two traitor calls, both lose it. Apply the stated exception even though ordinary payment happens at reveal.
changes.after: The winner of a traitor call keeps their committed spice and loses nothing. The betrayed player loses their committed spice. If both players call a traitor, both lose their spice.

changes.before: A winner's leader can move after a traitor victory
changes.after: Reusing a leader after a traitor win

changes.before: The new text explicitly releases the traitor winner's leader for use in another territory that round. Our older core book did not give that exception explicitly. Do not describe this as proof every older table played it differently.
changes.after: After winning with a traitor, you may use your leader in another territory that round. The earlier Dune Zone core book did not state this exception.

changes.before: Leaderlessness stays secret until reveal
changes.after: No advance leaderless announcement

changes.before: Previously you had to announce that no leader or Cheap Hero was available. The new book removes that advance disclosure. The absence still prevents Treachery cards in the battle plan.
changes.after: You no longer announce in advance that you have no available leader or Cheap Hero. Without either in your Battle Plan, you still cannot play Treachery cards in the battle.

changes.before: The source says include a leader or Cheap Hero if possible, but also describes being unwilling to use a Cheap Hero. Whether the card is compulsory when no leader disc is available needs clarification.
changes.after: One passage requires a leader or Cheap Hero whenever possible. Another describes a player being unwilling to use Cheap Hero. It is unclear whether you must play the card when no leader disc is available.

changes.before: Aftermath and negotiated surrender
changes.after: Battle results and surrender

changes.before: Earlier surviving leaders are exposed
changes.after: Lasgun/shield explosions kill earlier survivors

changes.before: In 2.0, a lasgun/shield explosion also kills face-up leaders that survived earlier battles in that territory. Our old GF9 book explicitly protected those earlier survivors as use markers. This is a change from that adopted ruling, not a clear reversal of an unambiguous sentence in the bare 2019 printing.
changes.after: A lasgun/shield explosion now kills face-up leaders that survived earlier battles in the territory. The earlier Dune Zone book protected those leaders, treating them as markers of where they had fought. The 2019 printing was less clear; this reverses Dune Zone's ruling.

changes.before: Your leader survives the first battle and remains beside the territory. The remaining rivals then detonate a lasgun and Shield. The new rule kills your earlier survivor too.
changes.after: Your leader survives a battle and remains beside the territory. If the remaining rivals then detonate a lasgun and Shield there, your leader dies too.

changes.before: Initiative is the familiar priority with clearer wording
changes.after: Initiative replaces aggressor

changes.before: The new name replaces aggressor. The player with Initiative still chooses its battles and wins ties. The new text expressly permits leaving a territory with multiple rivals, resolving a battle elsewhere, then returning to the first territory.
changes.after: The player with Initiative still chooses their battles and wins ties. The new rule also states that they may leave a territory containing several rivals, resolve a battle elsewhere, then return to the first territory.

changes.before: A winning plan does not preserve every card
changes.after: Cards after a victory

changes.before: Ordinary reusable weapons and defenses can still be kept where their text permits. Revealed Worthless cards and one-shot Actions do not follow that general retention habit. Cheap Hero was already discarded after use in the earlier FAQ.
changes.after: Reusable weapons and defenses can be kept when their text allows it. Revealed Worthless cards must now be discarded. One-use Actions are also discarded. The earlier FAQ already required Cheap Hero to be discarded after use.

changes.before: Still a Shield-specific explosion
changes.after: Which defenses cause an explosion?

changes.before: A kinetic defense is not automatically a Shield. Weirding Way does not cause the explosion; Shield-Snooper does. That distinction was already in the expansion rules and our old books.
changes.after: Lasgun explodes against Shield or Shield-Snooper. Weirding Way used as a kinetic defense does not cause an explosion. This distinction was already in the expansion rules and earlier Dune Zone books.

changes.before: An explicit agreement template
changes.after: Negotiated Surrender

changes.before: The new book describes Negotiated Surrender rather than leaving players to infer every part from the general deal rule. Both players agree on the thrown battle and its legal terms. The template normally avoids weapons, defenses and traitor calls, while allowing agreed Worthless disposal. Legal deals already permitted deliberate losses; the new book supplies an explicit template.
changes.after: The new book describes how to agree on a deliberately lost battle. Both players agree on a legal plan and its terms. The usual agreement excludes weapons, defenses and traitor calls, but may allow Worthless cards to be discarded. Deliberate losses were already possible under the deal rules; the surrender section gives a procedure for them.

changes.before: What this does not change
changes.after: Legal limits still apply

changes.before: A deal cannot grant an illegal action or transfer cards, forces, leaders, tokens or advantages without a specific rule allowing it. A thrown battle is still resolved through a legal battle plan; it is not permission to teleport the losing force into reserves.
changes.after: A surrender agreement cannot allow illegal actions or transfers of cards, forces, leaders, tokens or advantages. Resolve the battle with a legal plan and the normal losses. Losing forces do not return to reserves simply because the loss was agreed.

changes.before: Resolve the agreed plan
changes.after: Agree on the losses

changes.before: Agree on a losing plan, then identify its force commitment, any legal card disposal and losses. Do not treat the negotiated outcome as an exemption from the printed restrictions.
changes.after: Before revealing, agree on the losing force dial and any permitted card disposal. The agreement remains subject to the surrender restrictions in the rulebook.

changes.before: Atreides can still build toward its token
changes.after: Atreides battle losses still count

changes.before: A legal thrown battle can contribute actual battle losses toward Kwisatz Haderach. The counter is now public. The example does not add storm or worm casualties to that counter.
changes.after: Losses in an agreed battle count toward Kwisatz Haderach. Atreides now tracks those losses publicly. Storm and worm losses still do not count.

changes.before: Harkonnen and expansion effects
changes.after: Post-battle effects

changes.before: The source's surrender template excludes specified post-battle effects such as the revised Moritani Execute. That name reference does not provide the full new expansion procedure. Use the actual effect and agreement, not a guessed generic "nothing triggers" rule.
changes.after: The surrender procedure excludes certain effects, including Moritani's revised Execute. The base book mentions that ability but does not give its complete new expansion rules. It does not establish a general rule that every post-battle ability is canceled by surrender.

changes.before: Unlock leader revival once
changes.after: Leader revival

changes.before: Ordinary revival opened once the faction's leaders were dead or otherwise covered by the clarified eligibility rule. A twice-killed revived leader went face down and waited for the rest of the roster's revival-and-death cycle.
changes.after: A faction became eligible to revive leaders after all its leaders were dead or otherwise unavailable under the clarified rules. A revived leader killed for a second time had to wait for the rest of the leaders to complete another revival-and-death cycle.

changes.before: When all of your leaders are dead or captured, ordinary leader revival unlocks. Put your second faction token in the Tanks as a reminder. After that, you may choose any dead leader for your one normal leader revival each round, including a leader you revived before.
changes.after: Once all your leaders are dead or captured, place your second faction token in the Tanks. From then on, you may revive any dead leader with your one normal leader revival each round. A leader who has already been revived is eligible again.

changes.before: Bring the same leader back
changes.after: Reviving the same leader again

changes.before: You unlock revival, revive your strongest leader, then it dies again. Next Revival you may pay for that leader again. You do not wait for every other leader to complete another cycle.
changes.after: After leader revival becomes available, you revive your strongest leader and it dies again. You may pay to revive that leader in the next Revival phase without waiting for the others to die again.

changes.before: What remains familiar
changes.after: Cost and limit stay the same

changes.before: Normal leader revival still costs the printed fighting strength and still allows only one leader in that phase. The leader remains subject to its original traitor card. Counting captured leaders toward opening revival was already clarified; the removal of the death cycle is the major change.
changes.after: Normal revival still costs the leader's fighting strength in spice, with one leader revival per phase. The leader is still subject to its original traitor card. Captured leaders already counted toward eligibility under the earlier clarifications.

changes.before: Special-force revivals
changes.after: Ghola can revive several special forces

changes.before: Ghola may now revive multiple starred forces. The old FAQ explicitly kept Ghola within the one-Fedaykin or one-Sardaukar limit. Ordinary revival still has that special-force cap. Emperor's revised one-time power has its own additional exception.
changes.after: Ghola may now revive multiple starred forces. The old FAQ limited it to one Fedaykin or Sardaukar. That cap still applies to normal revival. Emperor's revised once-per-game power also has an exception.

changes.before: Atreides token exception
changes.after: Kwisatz Haderach revival

changes.before: A dead Kwisatz Haderach can use your one leader revival for two spice even before ordinary leader revival unlocks. That explicitly reverses the eligibility requirement in our old book; it is not an extra revival.

The shipment discount applies to an allowed shipment and gives no extra Shipping action.

changes.before: Rates are not income
changes.after: Guild rates

changes.before: Receiving Guild rates means paying the discounted price for the permitted shipment. It does not mean collecting the Guild's revenue when another faction ships.
changes.after: The shipping effect reduces the shipment's price. It does not let you collect Guild income from another faction's shipment.

changes.before: The force threshold still applies
changes.after: Dial four, gain up to +2

changes.before: No unaffordable bluff bid
changes.after: Bids must be affordable

changes.after: The old Karama clarification allowed bids beyond your spice holdings while you held Karama. The new auction rule forbids unaffordable bids, even with Solaris. You can instead take the current card for free on your own bidding turn.

changes.before: Open wording: shipping scope
changes.after: Open wording: shipment types

changes.after: The card face specifies shipment from reserves. The explanation refers more broadly to any Shipping action. It is unclear whether Solaris can discount cross-shipping or a return to reserves.

changes.after: Solaris pays for spice strength, which Classic replaces with force support. The rulebook gives no equivalent payment rule for Classic.

changes.after: Other Treachery card changes

changes.before: Truthtrance concerns information
changes.after: Truthtrance asks for information

changes.before: The old FAQ allowed a binding decision about an action later that turn. The new explanation limits Truthtrance to information the player can answer truthfully. Do not ask it to bind a future shipment or a future decision.
changes.after: The old FAQ allowed Truthtrance to bind a player to a decision later that turn. It now asks for information the player can answer truthfully. It cannot bind a future shipment or decision.

changes.before: Not through the new Truthtrance rule. Ask a question about information instead. A separate legal deal has its own rules and cannot turn the card into its old future-commitment power.
changes.after: No. Truthtrance now asks for information rather than a promise about a future action. A separate deal may bind a player under the deal rules.

changes.before: Do not use unanswerable questions as a search engine
changes.after: Unanswerable questions

changes.before: The source handles genuinely unanswerable questions without consuming the card, but forbids deliberately probing every possible traitor with questions designed to produce "I don't know" answers.
changes.after: A genuinely unanswerable question does not consume Truthtrance. Players cannot deliberately test a series of possible traitors by asking questions intended to produce "I don't know" answers.

changes.before: Revealed Worthless cards leave your hand
changes.after: Discard revealed Worthless cards

changes.after: A Worthless card may still fill a Weapon or Defense slot. Once revealed, discard it even if you win. The earlier Dune Zone book allowed winners to keep it.

changes.before: Keep these distinctions
changes.after: Other cards after battle

changes.before: Cheap Hero remains a zero-strength replacement for the leader, not a Weapon or Defense card. Used Cheap Hero disposal was already in the old FAQ. Winning reusable weapons and defenses are still generally retained unless their own text says otherwise.
changes.after: Cheap Hero is still a strength-zero replacement for a leader and is discarded after use, as required by the old FAQ. It does not fill a Weapon or Defense slot. Reusable weapons and defenses can still be kept after a win unless their own text says otherwise.

changes.before: Harj remains an extra move
changes.after: Harj, formerly Hajr

changes.before: The new spelling maps to old Hajr. It gives an additional on-planet movement immediately after your own normal movement, not another shipment. Reassessing ornithopters at the additional move was already clarified.
changes.after: Harj gives an additional on-planet move immediately after your normal movement. It gives no extra shipment. Checking ornithopters again for the additional move was already allowed by the earlier clarification.

changes.before: Resolve timing in storm order
changes.after: Weather Control and Family Atomics

changes.before: The old FAQ allowed Weather Control and Family Atomics in either played order. The new explanation permits one after the other only when that next player is later in storm order.
changes.after: The old FAQ allowed these cards in either order. The new explanation allows a second card after the first only if its player is later in storm order.

changes.before: Still familiar
changes.after: Shield Wall destruction

changes.before: Family Atomics still removes Shield Wall and exposes the protected areas to future storm movement. The storm does not retroactively sweep its current position just because the wall was destroyed. Its force or adjacency condition and round-one restriction are older rules.
changes.after: Family Atomics still removes Shield Wall, exposing the protected areas to later storm movement. The storm does not sweep its current position again when the wall is destroyed. The force or adjacency condition and round-one restriction are unchanged.

changes.before: Weather Control can be played before the Storm card is drawn. In that case no Storm card is drawn for that movement. Do not keep using only the old battle-wheel timing language.
changes.after: Weather Control can be played before the Storm card is drawn. If it is, no Storm card is drawn for that movement.

changes.before: Seat order matters
changes.after: Example of card order

changes.before: If the Family Atomics player is later in storm order than the player who just used Weather Control, the new explanation allows that sequence. A player earlier in the order cannot assume a free interrupt after a later player's card.
changes.after: After Weather Control is played, a player later in storm order may respond with Family Atomics. A player earlier in storm order cannot respond in that sequence.

changes.before: The base Treachery deck increases from 33 to 35 cards. Two Solaris cards are reported in the supplied physical material. Do not add an extra set of old replacement Karamas on top of the intended deck.
changes.after: The base Treachery deck increases from 33 to 35 cards. The supplied card images show two Solaris cards. The new deck does not require an extra set of the old replacement Karamas.

changes.before: Allies leave shared territory differently
changes.after: Allies sharing a territory

changes.before: The first ally taking its turn could remain; the later ally had to leave or lose its forces to the Tanks. Our old book preserved that explicit ally rule.
changes.after: After forming an alliance in a shared territory, the first ally could stay. The later ally had to leave or lose its forces to the Tanks.

changes.before: After a Nexus leaves you sharing a territory, the first faction with a Movement action must leave. If it cannot, those forces return to reserves at the end of its turn. If both somehow remain by phase end, the co-occupying forces return to reserves. The fallback is no longer a casualty in the Tanks.
changes.after: The first ally with a Movement action must leave the shared territory. If it cannot, its forces return to reserves at the end of its turn. If both allies remain at phase end, the forces sharing the territory return to reserves. They no longer go to the Tanks.

changes.before: A first mover without a legal exit
changes.after: The first ally cannot leave

changes.before: Your new ally shares the territory. You act first but cannot move out. Under the new written procedure your forces return to reserves; you do not simply stay and force your later ally to solve it.
changes.after: You form an alliance while sharing a territory. You act first but have no legal move out. Your forces return to reserves at the end of your turn; your ally does not have to leave instead.

changes.before: Normal ally payments are retained
changes.after: Allied payments

changes.before: You may still make the permitted contributions to an ally's auction purchase or shipment. That does not create a shared purse and does not permit ordinary allied battle-spice payments.
changes.after: You may still contribute to an ally's auction purchase or shipment as permitted by those rules. Ordinary allied contributions cannot pay for battle spice.

changes.before: The old FAQ allowed shipping into an ally's territory if you moved out afterward. The new rule forbids ending an action there, and Shipment and Movement are distinct actions. A literal reading removes that old sequence; the exact old example is not addressed explicitly.
changes.after: The old FAQ allowed shipping into an ally's territory if you moved out afterward. The new rule forbids ending an action there, and Shipment and Movement are separate actions. Read literally, it forbids the old sequence, but the rulebook does not address that example directly.

changes.before: The specific advisor rules permit the intended coexistence with an ally. Use those rules rather than treating advisors as ordinary co-occupying fighters. The general alliance paragraph does not repeat the exception, which remains flagged in this guide.
changes.after: Bene Gesserit advisors have specific rules allowing them to stay with an ally. The general alliance paragraph does not repeat this exception. See the Bene Gesserit pages and the unresolved wording section.

changes.before: Still blocked
changes.after: Occupied strongholds

changes.before: A stronghold occupied by two other factions still blocks ordinary entry and passage. The rare-case explanations are not a normal invitation for a third faction to enter.
changes.after: A stronghold occupied by two other factions still blocks ordinary entry and passage. The exceptional cases described in the rulebook do not allow a third faction to enter normally.

changes.before: The unified game includes bribery
changes.after: Bribery is part of the default game

changes.before: Bribery appeared in the old printing but the later FAQ and our book treated it as Advanced. It is now part of the default game. State nonally deals aloud; those legal deals are binding and need not include a spice bribe.
changes.after: The old FAQ and Dune Zone book treated bribery as Advanced, although it appeared in the old printing. It is now part of the default game. Announce deals with non-allies aloud. Legal deals are binding and do not have to include a spice bribe.

changes.before: Allied promises are different
changes.after: Deals between allies

changes.before: Deals between allies are expressly nonbinding and cannot themselves transfer spice. The normal permitted allied payments and specific Emperor exception still work. Do not treat an alliance promise like a public binding nonally bargain.
changes.after: Allied deals are nonbinding and cannot transfer spice. The usual allied contributions and Emperor's specific gift ability still apply.

changes.before: Payment is still deferred
changes.after: Bribes are paid later

changes.before: Bribe spice waits in front of the recipient's screen until the start of Mentat Pause. That delay, void impossible terms and unanimous cancellation were already clarified in the earlier game.
changes.after: Bribe spice stays in front of the recipient's screen until the start of Mentat Pause. This delay is unchanged. The earlier rules also made impossible terms void and allowed deals to be canceled by unanimous agreement.

changes.before: The new book expressly forbids both. Finish those actions before the phase begins. Old "any time" card wording is not a blanket override of this new phase restriction.
changes.after: Players cannot make new bribes or play Treachery cards during Mentat Pause. The new phase restriction applies even to cards with older "any time" wording.

changes.before: You may keep information secret, but everyone must know that an exchange is taking place, including private messages or leaving the room to talk. Concealing the contents and concealing the transaction are different.
changes.after: Private information exchanges must be announced, including private messages and conversations outside the room. The contents may remain secret, but the exchange itself must be public.

changes.before: General notes are now prohibited
changes.after: Only Atreides may take notes

changes.before: The old FAQ and our GF9 book allowed general notes while reserving Treachery tracking to Atreides. The new default forbids notes except the Atreides Bidding advantage.
changes.after: The new default forbids written notes except through Atreides' Bidding advantage. The old FAQ and Dune Zone book allowed general notes, while reserving Treachery card tracking to Atreides.

changes.before: Discard piles cannot be searched without permission. That was already in our GF9 book. Watching a public discard happen is different from searching the pile later.
changes.after: Searching discard piles still requires permission, as in Dune Zone's earlier book. Players may still watch public discards as they happen.

changes.after: City income

changes.after: During Spice Collection, the controlling faction receives two spice for Arrakeen, two for Carthag and one for Tuek's Sietch. These were Advanced rules in the earlier game; they are now part of the default.

changes.before: Carryalls is a familiar benefit with a name
changes.after: Carryalls

changes.after: Carryalls is the new name for the existing three-spice-per-force collection rate from qualifying city occupation. It does not add a second city income payment.

changes.after: City income is paid during Spice Collection, but the glossary defines control at round end. A sole occupant qualifies; the timing for storm-separated rivals is unclear. See the unresolved wording section.

changes.after: Stronghold targets are unchanged

changes.after: An unallied faction normally needs three strongholds. A two-faction alliance normally needs four. Victory is still checked during Mentat Pause.

changes.after: Choosing between qualifying winners

changes.after: Compare strongholds, then forces in strongholds, then spice. Apply these tie-breaks only after checking the priority order.

changes.after: Special victories

changes.after: Bene Gesserit prediction, Fremen's condition and Guild's revised condition have their own rules. The table covers normal victories. Some overlaps with special victories remain unclear.

changes.after: Guild must control strongholds

changes.after: Guild no longer wins simply by preventing another victory until game end. Its special victory now requires enough strongholds. Fremen's revised special condition also accounts for its ally. Check both before using the general round-ten tie-breaks.

changes.after: If no normal or special victory applies

Do not import the old no-Guild automatic Fremen fallback or our old inferred special-victory order.
changes.after: Compare strongholds. If tied, favor an unallied faction over an alliance, then compare forces in controlled strongholds, then spice. This replaces the old automatic Fremen fallback without Guild and Dune Zone's earlier inferred order for special victories.

changes.before: The new text stops after equal spice and does not fully settle every special-condition overlap. Those gaps remain visible in this guide.
changes.after: The rulebook gives no further tie-break after equal spice. It also leaves some overlaps between special victory conditions unresolved.

changes.before: Solo Guild tied with one faction
changes.after: Unallied Guild example

changes.after: Guild has two strongholds. Atreides has two and its Bene Gesserit ally has one. Guild meets its special condition because it matches the highest individual faction, despite the opposing alliance having three in total.

changes.after: 2019 roster illustrations pp2-3 and Advanced p13; second edition pp4-5,16-18. Names checked against the clearer scan.

changes.after: Leader changes

changes.after: Fremen and Harkonnen keep their five leaders and values. The other Atreides values remain 5,5,4,1. The other four Bene Gesserit leaders remain strength 5.

changes.after: Four ordinary forces and a surviving Duncan total 6 in Basic. In Advanced, the same total requires four spice to support the forces. Duncan contributes 2 in either case.

changes.after: Four force strength and a surviving Duncan total 7 without spice, or 9 after buying +2 for four spice. His higher value also affects the bounty for killing him and the cost to revive him.

changes.before: Do not add his point twice
changes.after: Duncan contributes 3

changes.after: Advanced setup and abilities are now standard

changes.after: After Fremen sets up, place one force in a territory of your choice. It is a fighter if alone or an advisor if sharing. This was the Advanced setup. Advisors and Advanced faction abilities are now part of the default game.

changes.before: Voice controls weapon or defense types
changes.after: Voice names weapon or defense types

changes.before: Name kinetic, poison or special for the relevant slot. It no longer controls Cheap Hero, Worthless or Reinforcements. changes.after: Name kinetic, poison or special for the relevant slot. Voice no longer controls Cheap Hero, Worthless or Reinforcements. The older FAQ required exact special-card names; the new rule allows the general special type. A weapon command cannot require or forbid Cheap Hero.

changes.before: Printed labels govern matching
changes.after: Use the printed card types

changes.after: A card labeled both special and kinetic or poison matches either type. An effect alone does not give a card another type. The new Gas Tooth example requires a special-weapon command.

changes.before: Do not force an optional role conversion
changes.after: Optional card roles

changes.after: Voice cannot force Weirding Way to act as a defense or Chemistry to act as a weapon. Their alternate roles remain optional, as clarified in the old game.

changes.after: Worthless cards can be used as either Karama or Solaris. Bene Gesserit keeps the economic effects and can use the new Bank-funded spice strength. A Worthless card used as Karama has the same restricted cancellation targets as a normal Karama.

changes.before: Cancellation window
changes.after: Canceling Voice

changes.after: Play Karama immediately after Bene Gesserit declares Voice, before the command takes effect.

changes.after: Prediction excludes titled special victories

changes.after: The old sheet excluded the Guild and Fremen special victories. The new rule excludes any victory through an advantage titled Special Victory Condition, including expansion abilities with that title.

changes.before: Normal victory is still predictable
changes.after: Predicting a normal victory

changes.after: The predicted faction may win alone or in an alliance, including with Bene Gesserit. This is unchanged. How prediction interacts with some round-ten results and overlapping special victories remains unclear.

changes.before: Voice still precedes Atreides Prescience. Advisors still do not fight, collect, block, confer ornithopters or supply the force permission for Family Atomics.
changes.after: Voice still comes before Atreides Prescience. Advisors still cannot fight, collect spice, block, grant ornithopters or count as the forces needed to play Family Atomics.

changes.before: Two-spice Charity is old Advanced
changes.after: CHOAM Charity

changes.after: Bene Gesserit receives two spice regardless of its current holdings, as under the old Advanced rules. The new wording also applies effects that modify CHOAM Charity to this amount.

changes.before: No separate one-time Karama
changes.after: No once-per-game Karama power

changes.after: Bene Gesserit still has no faction-specific once-per-game Karama power. Transmutation can be used repeatedly with Worthless cards. Spirit World does not add a one-time power.

changes.before: Expansion detail stays provisional
changes.after: CHOAM expansion rules are incomplete

changes.after: The new Bene Gesserit sheet allows Charity modifiers to affect its income. It does not give the updated CHOAM faction effects, amounts or payment times.

changes.before: Bene Gesserit: plan your face changes
changes.after: Bene Gesserit: advisors and fighters

changes.after: Advisors no longer flip when left alone

changes.after: Under the old Advanced rules, advisors automatically became fighters when left alone. They now stay advisors. You may change them to fighters before Shipping and Movement begins, or during the stated setup exception.

changes.before: The old mid-move flip is gone
changes.after: No advisor-to-fighter change on arrival
